subject: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?

messages.author: b5f4802dc12ec04d
messages.subject: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?
parts:
Hi all,

I'm working through some mark-recapture data for basic survival estimates and trying to add complexity with some variables of interest. In this dataset, we have sex, age, and categorical site data. When working through examples in the AHM and IPM books (which are incredibly helpful!) there's usually a note that you *can* add complexity with covariates but not really how to do that. 

My goal is to get estimates of age class-specific survival across three different sites. 

I ran it with the linear model looking like:
logit(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu + beta.age*age[i,t] + beta.site2*site2[i] + beta.site3*site3[i] 

Where age is an array of 0 = juvenile, 1 = adult and site2/3 are dummy variables, therefore phi.mu is juvenile at site 1. 

It technically works but the estimates aren't tracking with the prior model I ran to just get adult site-specific estimates (where I used site as the only predictor therefore the identity link). 

So, with multiple categorical predictors, both time-dependent (age) and just individual-dependent (site doesn't change), is there a different way the linear model should be coded? 

Alternatively, should I create a grouping variable, one for each of the six combinations (2 ages, 3 sites?) This  method is how I got site and sex specific survival when I used the adults only. 


The bigger picture question I haven't found the answer to exactly is how JAGS understands when a 1, 2, 3 is group 1 etc., (as in, site[1]) as opposed to a numerical predictor value of 1, 2, or 3. Is this all in the choice of link in the linear model? Does adding more than one predictor automatically necessitate a logit or other link function?

Thanks in advance from a beleaguered recent MS grad who feels a bit out of her depth!

Stephanie

messages.author: bfa4a88c8a5bc54e
messages.subject: Re: Multiple categorical variables - link function in CJS?
parts: It technically works but the estimates aren't tracking with the prior model I ran to just get adult site-specific estimates (where I used site as the only predictor therefore the identity link).

I'm not exactly sure what you mean, but when you're adding any predictors at all, you should be using the logit-link. So even with just site, it should be:

logit(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu +  beta.site2*site2[i] + beta.site3*site3[i] 

Alternatively, and this gets to one of your other questions, if you have an (unordered) categorical predictor, you're essentially just estimating three intercepts. So you could formulate this as:

(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu[site[i]], 

where site[i] is a predictor variable taking on the values 1, 2, or 3 for the three sites. Each individual has its own site covariate so you get three indices in phi.mu. The prior would be:

for (i in 1:n_site) {
   phi.mu[i] ~ dlogis(0, 1)
}

Or some such.
So, with multiple categorical predictors, both time-dependent (age) and just individual-dependent (site doesn't change), is there a different way the linear model should be coded?

If you want a separate estimate for each age * site combination, you could do:

logit(phi[i,t]) <- phi.mu[site[i],age[i,t]],  # actually, with this specification you don't need the logit link, because each probability is getting estimated separately!

where age[i,t] is a time-varying individual covariate (e.g., at time 1 it may be a juvenile "1" and at time t-1 it might be adult "2"). Then the prior becomes:

for (i in 1:n_site) {
   for (j in 1:n_age) {
      phi.mu[i,j] ~ dlogis(0, 1)  # with logit-link
#      phi.mu[i,j] ~ dbeta(1, 1)  # without logit-link

}
}

The bigger picture question I haven't found the answer to exactly is how JAGS understands when a 1, 2, 3 is group 1 etc., (as in, site[1]) as opposed to a numerical predictor value of 1, 2, or 3. Is this all in the choice of link in the linear model? Does adding more than one predictor automatically necessitate a logit or other link function?

I struggled to understand this for a while as well. JAGS doesn't know anything about what each number means; it's about how you code it. If you have beta * x[i] it fits a single coefficient through that cloud of predictors vs. response. If you index coefficients by the values therein, e.g., beta[x[i]], it estimates separate betas for each value of x. Does that make sense? Btw, there are other link functions available, but yes, you'll need a link function most of the time because you can't let the probabilities go outside of [0,1]. Another good link function is the loglog-link. This estimates your survival probabilities as mortality rates, which has many nice properties including being able to deal quite well with unequal time intervals in multistate models (see https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13059).

Hope this helps (and that I was correct).

Matt
